title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (1 of 7)
hook: a new camp opens with a text so short it fits on one page

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita closed: eighteen chapters, and your line was you actually read it. Today the path goes underneath it.

Eighteen verses. It fits on one page, and people have written whole books about its first line. It's one of the Upanishads, the older texts underneath the Gita, the ones it draws on: the Gita quotes them, borrows their pictures, sometimes their exact verses. Many texts carry the name, and tradition sets apart a small group as the principal ones. Camp five, the depths, spends a week each on four of them, starting with one of the shortest.
screen: `EIGHTEEN VERSES.` → `UNDERNEATH THE GITA.` → `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.`

segments.voice: The word Upanishad is usually explained as sitting down near: upa, near, ni, down, shad, to sit. A student sitting close to a teacher, close enough to hear something said quietly. That's the feel of these texts. Not a law code, not a hymnbook. A conversation near the fire. The Isha Upanishad is named after its first word. Isha means the Lord, the one who rules. The verse opens: isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is vasyam by the Lord. That one word, vasyam, can be read two ways. Some commentators read it as dwelt in, pervaded: the Lord lives inside everything, the way salt lives in seawater. The great teacher Shankara read it as covered, clothed: wrap everything you see in the thought of the Lord, the way you'd wrap a gift. Either way, the claim is enormous. Not some things. All this. The coffee cup. The traffic. The person you find difficult. The second half of the verse is where this week's word comes from, and it's tomorrow's lesson. But hold the first half for a day, because everything else in the Upanishad leans on it. If all this belongs to the Lord, then nothing here is only mine. And nothing here is only ordinary. Mahatma Gandhi is often quoted as saying that if all the other scriptures were lost and only this first verse remained, Hinduism would live on. That's a lot of weight for one line. This week will show whether it can carry it.
screen: `UPANISHAD: SITTING DOWN NEAR.` · `ISHA: THE LORD.` · `DWELT IN, OR CLOTHED.` · `NOT SOME THINGS. ALL THIS.` · then, large: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of you, a wall, a window, your own hands, and try the verse on it: all this; whatever your tradition calls the sacred, or simply life itself, imagine it living inside the thing you're looking at. Then close your eyes and try it on the sounds around you, then on your own breath. If you pray, you can say the two words isha vasyam quietly; if not, just notice.
Isha, the Lord, the one who rules. Today, the first half of the Isha's first verse: all this, whatever moves, is pervaded by the Lord. Tomorrow, the renouncing and the enjoying.
Your line: nothing here is only mine. For today, just the ground under it. Day two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Hindus know the Isha Upanishad's first verse by heart, and it is often chanted along with the 'purnam adah' peace invocation that traditionally opens the text.
